Abstract
Vision-language models transfer well in zero-shot settings, but at
deployment the visual and textual branches often shift asymmet-
rically. Under this condition, entropy-based test-time adaptation
can sharpen the fused posterior while increasing error, because an
unreliable modality may still dominate fusion. We study this failure
mode through a majorization view of multimodal posteriors and
cast adaptation as a constrained de-mixing problem on the fused
prediction. Based on this view, we propose MG-MTTA, which keeps
the backbone frozen and updates only a lightweight gate or adapter.
The objective combines fused-posterior entropy minimization with
a reliability-aware gate prior built from anchor-based modality con-
sistency and cross-modal conflict. Our analysis gives conditions
under which entropy reduction preserves the correct ranking and
a threshold that characterizes modality-dominance failure. On the
ImageNet-based benchmark, MG-MTTA improves top-1 accuracy
from 57.97 to 66.51 under semantics-preserving textual shift and
from 21.68 to 26.27 under joint visual-textual shift, while remaining
competitive in the visual-only benchmark. These results show that
multimodal test-time adaptation should control modality reliability,
not just prediction entropy.

Introduction
Vision-language models (VLMs) have become a standard founda-
tion for multimodal recognition, retrieval, and open-vocabulary
understanding. Their large-scale pretraining substantially improves
zero-shot transfer and cross-modal reasoning across diverse tasks.
However, realistic deployment rarely preserves the source-domain
conditions seen during pretraining [3, 14]. Instead, the two modal-
ities are often perturbed asymmetrically: the visual stream may
suffer from blur, occlusion, low illumination, or style shift, while the
textual stream may exhibit prompt-template drift, lexical variation,
or other forms of semantics-preserving phrasing shift [3, 21, 29].
The resulting challenge is therefore not merely uncertainty under
a single distribution shift, but multimodal decision-making under
modality-specific shift.
This asymmetry creates a failure mode that is specific to multi-
modal fusion. When one modality becomes unreliable but remains
artificially sharp, entropy minimization can further increase confi-
dence in an incorrect fused decision [25]. In other words, a lower-
entropy posterior is not necessarily a better posterior once fusion is
driven by modality imbalance. A satisfactory test-time adaptation
method for VLMs should therefore do more than sharpen predic-
tions: it should identify when entropy reduction corresponds to
genuine recovery and when it merely amplifies the influence of a
corrupted modality.
Our starting point is to view modality-specific shift through pos-
terior geometry. We model each modality-level posterior as a doubly
stochastic mixing of an underlying clean posterior, up to a residual
that captures deviation from the idealized mixing model [10]. Under
this view, test-time adaptation becomes a constrained de-mixing
problem on the fused posterior. This perspective is useful for two
reasons. First, it provides a principled explanation of why entropy
may increase under shift and why a successful update should re-
verse that trend only along a valid majorization direction [10, 17].
Second, it exposes the role of modality reliability in fusion: if one
stream is poorly explained by the mixing model or conflicts sharply
with the other stream, its contribution should be downweighted
during adaptation [15, 28]. Throughout the paper, we distinguish
between an ideal analysis object based on doubly stochastic mixing
and its practical implementation. The former clarifies the majoriza-
tion geometry of multimodal degradation and recovery, whereas
the latter is realized by a computable modality-to-anchor reliability
proxy built from running anchors.
Based on this formulation, we propose a majorization-guided
test-time adaptation method that keeps the vision-language back-
bone frozen and updates only a lightweight gate or adapter module.
The method combines entropy minimization on the fused posterior
with reliability-aware regularization derived from two computable
signals: an anchor-based reliability proxy inspired by doubly sto-
chastic fit, and a cross-modality disagreement proxy that reflects
conflict between the two streams. The resulting objective keeps the
trainable subset small and is directly aligned with the theoretical
quantities used in our analysis.

Our contributions are summarized as follows.
• We identify a multimodal-specific failure mode of entropy-
based test-time adaptation under modality-specific shift,
where lower entropy can reflect confidence amplification
by a biased modality rather than genuine recovery.
• We formulate this problem as a multimodal posterior de-
mixing problem based on majorization and doubly stochas-
tic mixing, and derive conditions under which entropy re-
duction is beneficial together with a modality-dominance
threshold that characterizes a concrete failure regime.
• We propose a lightweight adaptation method that updates
only a gate or adapter module while keeping the pretrained
backbone frozen, using reliability-aware regularization based
on an anchor-based reliability proxy and cross-modality
disagreement.
• We establish an evaluation protocol that separates visual
shift, semantics-preserving textual shift, and joint shift,
while treating conflicting textual perturbations as failure
analysis rather than as part of the main robustness bench-
mark.
2
Related Work
2.1
Test-Time Adaptation
Test-time adaptation (TTA) aims to adapt a source model to un-
labeled target data at inference time without full retraining [7].
Representative methods reduce predictive entropy, update normal-
ization statistics, stabilize predictions with teacher models, filter
unreliable samples, or restrict adaptation to small parameter sub-
sets for robustness [11, 12, 22, 23]. These approaches have been
especially effective in image classification, where the model output
is usually treated as a single posterior to be sharpened or stabilized
under shift.
The multimodal case is more delicate. Once prediction depends
on both visual and textual streams, lower entropy does not by itself
imply a better decision. The outcome also depends on whether
fusion remains aligned with the more reliable modality. This dif-
ference motivates the setting considered here, where the visual
posterior, the textual posterior, and the fused posterior are treated
as separate but coupled objects.

2.2
Vision-Language Models under Shift and
Test-Time Adaptation
Vision-language models built on contrastive pretraining and large-
scale multimodal learning have substantially improved transfer
across recognition, retrieval, and open-vocabulary tasks [1, 16, 26].
At the same time, their predictions remain sensitive to prompt de-
sign, visual corruptions, and broader distribution shift [4, 13, 24].
Existing studies have mainly documented this sensitivity through
performance degradation, calibration, or prompt robustness anal-
yses [3, 14], making clear that robustness remains fragile once
deployment conditions depart from pretraining.
Recent work has therefore extended TTA to vision-language and
multimodal models through prompt tuning, lightweight adaptation,
or reliability-aware correction [5, 9, 18, 25]. These methods are
the closest practical neighbors to our setting because they adapt
frozen or lightly updated multimodal backbones under target shift.
Still, most existing formulations are organized around entropy min-
imization, consistency, or heuristic reliability adjustment. Although
robustness is evaluated on the fused prediction, the fused posterior
itself is usually not treated as the object of analysis. As a result,
current methods say relatively little about when entropy reduction
preserves the correct fused ranking and when it instead reinforces
a biased modality. Our formulation focuses on this point directly
by studying multimodal adaptation at the fused-posterior level.
2.3
Fusion, Reliability, and Majorization
A separate line of work studies multimodal fusion under modal-
ity imbalance and shows that reliability-aware weighting can im-
prove prediction by reducing the influence of noisy or misaligned
streams [6, 20, 27, 28]. This line of research provides an impor-
tant practical intuition for our setting: when the modalities are not
equally trustworthy, robust fusion should not weight them equally.
Separately, majorization theory provides a natural language for
describing how probability vectors become more mixed or less
mixed [10]. While it is closely related to entropy and posterior
geometry, it has rarely been used to study multimodal adaptation.
In this paper, majorization is not used only as a descriptive tool.
It is also used to clarify when entropy reduction corresponds to
genuine recovery and when a sharper prediction is simply a sharper
mistake under modality-specific shift.
3
Method
MG-MTTA adapts a frozen vision-language model by updating only
a lightweight fusion module at test time. For each test sample, the
model first produces visual and textual predictions, then estimates
modality reliability from running anchors and cross-modality con-
flict, and finally regularizes the fusion gate toward the more reliable
modality. The fused prediction is optimized with entropy minimiza-
tion, gate regularization, and batch diversity. The rest of this section
first states the practical adaptation rule used in deployment and
then introduces the majorization-based mixing view that motivates
it.

4
Experiments
4.1
Experimental Setup
We evaluate MG-MTTA under three test regimes: visual shift, semantics-
preserving textual shift, and joint shift. The visual setting serves to
anchor the method to standard corruption benchmarks, while the
textual and joint settings more directly test the multimodal fusion
failures that motivate this paper. We further use diagnostic analy-
ses and failure cases to examine whether the observed behavior is
consistent with the proposed majorization-based view.
4.1.1
Benchmarks and shift construction. All main-text experiments
are instantiated under a shared ImageNet label space, which allows
visual, textual, and joint shift to be compared within a single proto-
col.
Visual robustness is evaluated on CIFAR-100C and ImageNet-C
from the common-corruptions benchmark family [4]. Unless other-
wise stated, we report mean top-1 accuracy over the 15 corruption
types at severity level 5. This part mainly serves as a benchmark-
anchoring comparison to existing CLIP test-time adaptation results.
The textual setting is constructed differently. We keep the image
fixed and perturb only the prompt bank, while preserving class iden-
tity. The L1–L4 ladder is not built from arbitrary prompt rewrites.
Instead, it is motivated by the input-processing mechanism of CLIP-
style text encoders, whose representations are sensitive to token
boundaries, character-level perturbations, and local prompt con-
text. We therefore apply label-preserving token- and context-level
perturbations that progressively destabilize the text representation
without changing the underlying class semantics. The resulting
perturbations include prompt-template drift, lexical substitution,
and removal of non-essential modifiers, and are averaged into a
unified textual-shift score over the same ImageNet label space.
Joint shift combines image corruption with the semantics-preserving
textual perturbations above. By contrast, prompt perturbations

main benchmark and reserved for failure analysis, because they

Limitations
MG-MTTA is designed for modality-specific shift, especially textual
and joint regimes where asymmetric fusion errors dominate. On
visual-only corruption benchmarks, it is competitive with matched
entropy-based variants but not the strongest external CLIP adapta-
tion baseline. The method relies on running anchors and a calibrated
semantics-preserving textual stress protocol. Runtime and memory
overhead are not separately quantified in this version, so efficiency
claims are limited to the small trainable parameter subset.
6
Conclusion
This paper studies test-time adaptation for vision-language models
under modality-specific shift. We formulate multimodal adapta-
tion as a de-mixing problem on the fused posterior and show that
entropy reduction alone is insufficient: it is useful only when the
adapted posterior follows a valid majorization-consistent direction
while preserving the decisive ranking. MG-MTTA implements this
view by keeping the CLIP ViT-B/16 backbone frozen and adapting
a lightweight gate or adapter with fused-posterior entropy mini-
mization, reliability-aware gate regularization, and batch diversity.
The diagnostics and failure cases are consistent with the proposed
explanation: entropy-only adaptation may sharpen the wrong fused
decision, whereas reliability-aware adaptation more often aligns

H
Prompt Construction and Textual Shift
Protocol
Our textual-shift design is guided by the text-processing mechanism
of CLIP-style vision–language models rather than by arbitrary
prompt rewriting. In CLIP/OpenCLIP-style models, the text branch
maps each prompt into a fixed-length token sequence and then
into a single text representation used for image–text matching.
This makes the model sensitive not only to prompt semantics, but
also to token boundaries, character-level perturbations, and local
prompt context. Motivated by this property, we construct a token-
level textual stress protocol that perturbs the prompt in ways that
remain largely label-preserving while progressively degrading the
stability of the text representation.
The textual-shift protocol is divided into two categories.
Semantics-preserving textual stress. This category is used in the
main experiments. Its goal is not to change the class label, but to
perturb the prompt at the token and local-context level in a con-
trolled manner. Compared with purely semantic paraphrasing, this
construction is more directly tied to how CLIP-style text encoders
tokenize and represent prompts. Accordingly, the main protocol
operates on token boundaries, character-level spelling noise, and
mild context degradation while preserving the underlying class
identity.
We instantiate a five-level token-level textual stress ladder:
• L1: context-only typo. Mild character-level perturbation
is applied to prompt-context words such as photo, image,
or picture, without modifying the class phrase itself.
• L2: context typo + class-boundary perturbation. In
addition to the L1 context perturbation, the class phrase is
modified at the boundary level, for example by replacing
spaces with hyphens or underscores, while avoiding inner-
token corruption.
• L3: partial mild class-token corruption. Based on L2, a
deterministic subset of classes receives an additional mild
inner-token perturbation on the class phrase. This increases
difficulty while retaining approximate human readability.
• L4: expanded class-token corruption with mild con-
text drop. Relative to L3, the subset of classes receiving
class-token corruption is enlarged, and the local grammat-
ical context is mildly degraded. This produces a stronger
but still label-preserving prompt shift.

Abstract: Vision-language models transfer well in zero-shot settings, but at deployment the visual and textual branches often shift asymmet- rically. Under this condition, entropy-based test-time adaptation can sharpen the fused posterior while increasing error, because an unreliable modality may still dominate fusion. We study this failure mode through a majorization view of multimodal posteriors and cast adaptation as a constrained de-mixing problem on the fused prediction. Based on this view, we propose MG-MTTA, which keeps the backbone frozen and updates only a lightweight gate or adapter. The objective combines fused-posterior entropy minimization with a reliability-aware gate prior built from anchor-based modality con- sistency and cross-modal conflict. Our analysis gives conditions under which entropy reduction preserves the correct ranking and a threshold that characterizes modality-dominance failure. On the ImageNet-based benchmark, MG-MTTA improves top-1 accuracy from 57.97 to 66.51 under semantics-preserving textual shift and from 21.68 to 26.27 under joint visual-textual shift, while remaining competitive in the visual-only benchmark. These results show that multimodal test-time adaptation should control modality reliability, not just prediction entropy.
